newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa's Zulu party pulls out of talks with ANC.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa's Zulu party pulls out of talks with ANC.

text.p: South Africa's Zulu- based Inkatha Freedom Party (IFP) on Friday withdrew from talks to end bitter decade-long turf wars with President Nelson Mandela's African National Congress (ANC).
Inkatha chairman Ben Ngubane cited the bias shown against his party at Truth and Reconciliation Commission (TRC) hearings this week as the main reason.
Mangosuthu Buthelezi, IFP leader and Home Affairs Minister in Mandela's cabinet, was accused at TRC hearings this week of knowing about killings carried out by IFP-aligned hit squads.
"Accordingly, we will no longer continue peace negotiations with the ANC until its leader demonstrates a commitent to peace and reconciliation," he told a news conference.
Buthelezi has denied any knowledge of hit squads alleged to have operated against his political enemies and said through his lawyers that he was "astounded" by the allegations.
A hit-squad leader has implicated Buthelezi's righthand man, Zakhele Khumalo, and several other senior party officials in the killing of supporters of their fiercest rival, the ANC.
"The IFP cannot in conscience continue peace talks with an organisation that is bent on destabilising this province for party-political gain," Ngubane said.
He said another means to deal with violence between the two parties would have to be found before peace talks could resume.
TRC commissioner Richard Lyster told reporters Inkatha had made a tragic decision to pull out of the peace talks.
"To blame the TRC for the collapse of the peace talks is shocking. We understand that they find the evidence coming out of these hearings difficult but they cannot blame us," he said.

The death toll in the troubled KwaZulu-Natal province, Buthelezi's stronghold, dropped after a peace treaty was signed just over a year ago, but human rights groups have said political killings are on the rise again.
More than 14,000 people have died in the conflict over the past decade.
The murder rate peaked at 338 in April 1994, when South Africans of all races voted together for the first time.
Since the beginning of the year, at least 98 people have been killed in an ongoing war. Independent conflict monitors have said they fear a renewed outbreak.

Ngubane said his party had called on Mandela to appoint a judicial commission of inquiry into alleged bias against Inkatha by the country's truth body, appointed in 1995 to heal the wounds of apartheid.

"The Inkatha Freedom Party will today (Friday) call on (Mandela) to appoint a judicial of inquiry into partiality of members of the Truth and Reconciliation Commission whose bias is threatening peace and the stability of the country," he said.
Presidential spokesman Parks Mankahlana told Reuters it was unlikely the request would be given serious consideration.
"I think that kind of suggestion is unlikely to receive serious consideration from the president," he said, adding in Mandela's opinion the truth commission had treated all parties equally.
